unit.title: Prepare for the application of protective coating

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why does a steel gate near the sea, for example in Port Royal, need a better coating system than the same gate far inland?
options: Sea air is cooler, so paint takes longer to dry
Salt in the air makes steel rust much faster
Sea air makes steel softer and easier to bend
Paint shops near the coast sell cheaper paint

questions.stem: Before you prepare a fabricated frame for painting, which document tells you the coating system, the surface preparation and the film thicknesses?
options: The welder's own notes on the cutting list
The supplier's delivery note for the steel
The client's receipt for the deposit paid
The coating specification for the job

questions.stem: Which information does a paint's technical data sheet give that you need when preparing to coat?
options: Surface preparation, mixing, thinning and drying times
The price of the paint at each of the hardware stores in town
The names of the factory workers who made the paint
Only the colour of the paint and the size of the tin

questions.stem: Which document should you read to find the fire, health and first-aid information for a primer?
options: The supplier's delivery note
The shop's price list
The safety data sheet (SDS)
The maker's colour chart

questions.stem: A new frame has oil, weld spatter and mill scale on it. Why is the oil removed BEFORE any grinding or blast cleaning?
options: Oil makes the grinding disc wear down too slowly
Grinding is easier and much safer on a greasy surface
Grinding or blasting would spread it over the steel
Oil can only be removed after the primer is on

questions.stem: Before a welded frame is coated, why are its sharp edges ground to a small radius?
options: Paint pulls thin on sharp edges and rust starts there
Rounded edges make the frame lighter to lift
Sharp edges make the paint dry too slowly
Paint is not sold for steel with sharp edges

questions.stem: Which fault on a finished weld should be put right before coating, because paint will not seal it well?
options: A weld that has been wire-brushed clean
A smooth weld with an even ripple on its face
A fillet weld of the correct leg length
Spatter and undercut along the weld toes

questions.stem: A frame made of closed hollow sections will be hot-dip galvanised. Why must vent and drain holes be made in it?
options: To make the frame lighter for the customer
Trapped air or water can burst it in the hot zinc
So the inspector can look at the welds inside
So that the zinc is kept out of the tubes

questions.stem: Why must every bit of slag be removed from the welds on a frame before it goes for hot-dip galvanising?
options: Slag makes the zinc coating far too thick
Slag melts into the zinc and changes its colour
Slag makes the frame too heavy for the bath
Zinc does not coat slag, so bare spots are left

questions.stem: Why should anti-spatter spray that contains silicone not be used on steel that will be painted or galvanised?
options: It makes the welds crack as they cool down
The coating will not stick where it remains
It turns the steel a dark colour after a day
It costs too much for use in a training shop

questions.stem: Which method removes mill scale and rust most completely before a high-performance coating?
options: Wiping with a damp rag
Hand wire brushing
Abrasive blast cleaning
Washing with fresh water

questions.stem: At the Centre, who may carry out abrasive blast cleaning, and where?
options: Only trained people, in a proper blast booth
Any trainee, in the open yard on a calm day
Anyone wearing safety glasses, in a weld bay
The cleaner, at the end of each working day

questions.stem: What is the 'surface profile' (also called the anchor pattern) left by blast cleaning?
options: Tiny peaks and valleys that help the paint grip
The colour of the steel just after it has been blasted
The shape of the steel section being coated
The thickness of paint on the finished job

questions.stem: How is the surface profile of a blasted plate usually checked before priming?
options: By running a finger across the surface
By weighing the plate before and after
With replica tape or a profile gauge
With a wet film comb on the bare steel

questions.stem: Blasted steel was left overnight in a humid shop and now shows a light orange rust. What should happen before it is primed?
options: Prime over it at once, as the rust is only light
Clean it again to the standard the job specifies
Wash it down with sea water to remove the rust
Put on one thicker coat of primer to hide all the rust

questions.stem: A specification says the steel must be at least 3 °C warmer than the dew point before coating. Why?
options: So the paint dries to a lighter colour
So the paint needs less thinner in the mix
So the brushes are easier to clean later
So no moisture forms on the steel under the paint

questions.stem: The air is 30 °C, the dew point is 26 °C and the steel is 27 °C. The rule is steel at least 3 °C above the dew point. Can coating start?
options: Yes, because the air is over 25 °C
No, the steel is only 1 °C above the dew point
Yes, because the steel is above the dew point
No, because the air is warmer than the steel

questions.stem: Which instrument gives you the readings needed to work out the relative humidity and dew point in the shop?
options: A wet film thickness comb
A spirit level and a tape
A surface profile gauge
A sling psychrometer or hygrometer

questions.stem: Why is early morning often a poor time to start coating steel that has stood outside overnight?
options: Dew may still be on the steel
Paint costs more before noon
The tins are too cold to open
Brushes are stiff in cool air

questions.stem: The end plates of a beam will be joined on site with friction-grip bolts. What should be done to their contact faces before coating?
options: Give them two extra coats of gloss paint
Grease them so the bolts tighten more easily
Mask them, or treat them as the specification says
Leave the mill scale on them to protect them

questions.stem: Why is the steel next to a joint that will be welded on site usually masked or left without the full coating?
options: Paint there would make the beam too heavy to lift
Masking tape protects that steel from the sunshine
The coating burns in the heat and spoils the weld
The site welder needs a clean place for his tools

questions.stem: What is the main job of the primer in a paint system?
options: To grip the steel and help stop corrosion
To give the final colour and the gloss
To fill wide gaps between badly fitted parts
To make the steel stronger under load

questions.stem: How does a zinc-rich primer protect the steel at a small scratch in the coating?
options: It hardens the steel around the scratch
It changes colour to warn of the damage
It seals the scratch with a rubbery skin
The zinc corrodes first, so the steel is spared

questions.stem: Why is a stripe coat brushed onto welds, edges and corners before the full coat is sprayed?
options: To mark the welds that the inspector must test
To build up film where spray coats are thin
To use up paint left over from the last job
To show the client which colour was chosen

questions.stem: What is the 'pot life' of a two-pack epoxy paint?
options: How long an unopened tin can be stored
How long the paint takes to dry hard
How many years the coating lasts outdoors
How long it stays usable after mixing

questions.stem: A two-pack paint is mixed with only half the hardener the data sheet gives. What is the likely result?
options: It dries faster and harder than normal
It may never cure properly, and will fail
It covers twice the area with one coat
It keeps for much longer in the tin before it is used

questions.stem: How much thinner may be added to a paint before it is applied?
options: Enough to make it run as freely as water
None ever, because thinner always spoils paint
Only the type and amount the data sheet allows
One full tin of thinner for each tin of paint

questions.stem: Why is paint stirred well, with a power mixer if needed, before use?
options: Solids settle and must be mixed back evenly
Stirring makes the paint dry more quickly
Stirring lets the thinner evaporate first
It is done only to check the colour is right

questions.stem: A topcoat with 65% volume solids is used with no thinner. The painter must reach 130 µm when dry. Which wet film reading should he aim for on his comb?
options: 200 µm
130 µm
85 µm
195 µm

questions.stem: A paint has 60% volume solids and is applied at 120 µm dry film thickness. What is its theoretical coverage?
options: 2 m² per litre
7.2 m² per litre
5 m² per litre
50 m² per litre

questions.stem: A frame has 24 m² to coat. The paint covers 6 m² per litre in theory, and the job allows 25% for losses. How many litres are needed?
options: 4 litres
5 litres
6 litres
3 litres

questions.stem: When is a wet film thickness comb used?
options: After the final coat has dried hard
Before any paint is mixed, on bare steel
On the tin, to see how full the tin is
Straight after applying, on the wet film

questions.stem: A data sheet gives a minimum and a maximum overcoat time for a primer. What can happen if the next coat goes on after the maximum time?
options: The two coats will blend into a new colour
The next coat may not stick properly
The primer will start to drip and run
The steel will need to be blasted twice

questions.stem: How should tins of paint and thinner be stored in a fabrication workshop?
options: On the welding bench, ready for use
Out in the sun, so the paint stays thin
In a closed office near the computers
In a cool, ventilated store away from sparks

questions.stem: Why must welding and grinding stop near an area where solvent-based paint is being mixed or sprayed?
options: Sparks can set the solvent vapour alight
Sparks change the colour of the wet paint
Grinding dust makes the paint dry too fast
Arc light makes the paint go bad in the tin

questions.stem: Which PPE suits a person mixing and brushing a solvent-based epoxy primer in the shop?
options: A welding helmet and a leather apron
Ear plugs and a paper dust mask, with no gloves at all
Chemical gloves, eye protection, a suitable respirator
Shorts and a cap, since the shop is hot

questions.stem: What is the main reason a coating area must be well ventilated?
options: To keep the paint tins cool and dry
To dry the brushes quickly between coats
To keep solvent vapour below harmful levels
To blow dust away onto the next job

questions.stem: Paint splashes into a worker's eye while mixing. What is the right first action?
options: Flush it with clean water for some minutes; get help
Rub the eye firmly with a clean rag to get it out
Wipe the eye with a little thinner to dissolve it
Cover the eye and finish the mix before reporting it

questions.stem: You must recoat an old steel gate that may have lead-based paint on it. What should happen before anyone grinds it?
options: Grind it quickly so the dust has no time to spread
Burn the old paint off with a cutting torch
Sand it dry outdoors with no mask on
Have it tested and follow a safe removal method

questions.stem: What should be done with rags soaked in solvent paint at the end of the day?
options: Leave them in a pile in a corner of the shop
Put them in a closed metal bin for safe disposal
Burn them in the yard with the other rubbish
Wash them in the sink and use them again

questions.stem: What must be checked before an airless spray pump is used?
options: That the spray tip has been taken off the gun
That the hose has been tied in a tight loop
That the pump is set to its highest pressure
Hose, tip guard and trigger lock, as the maker says

questions.stem: Why must you never point an airless spray gun at your hand, or wipe its tip while it is under pressure?
options: The paint would be wasted on the floor
The jet can inject paint into the skin
The tip would be blocked by the paint
It would make the spray pattern uneven

questions.stem: Why are surface preparation, weather and film thickness readings written on a coating record?
options: So the painter is paid for each reading
So the paint supplier can raise its price
To show the work met the specification
So the record can replace the data sheet

questions.stem: As team leader, what should you plan first before preparing a large frame for coating in the shop?
options: The order of work, access, ventilation and drying space
Which music the team will play during the work
How to finish the job without reading the data sheets
Who will take the leftover paint home afterwards

questions.stem: Steel stored near the sea is to be coated. Why might the specification ask for a test for salts on the surface?
options: Salt under the paint draws in water and causes blisters
Salt makes the steel far too heavy to lift and move safely
Salt changes the colour of the topcoat over time
Salt makes the paint dry in half the usual time

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the temperature at which moisture in the air starts to condense on a cool surface?
What is the name of the instrument with a wet-bulb and a dry-bulb thermometer that is whirled to find the relative humidity?
Some data sheets say a mixed two-pack paint must stand for a set time before use. What is this time called?
What do the letters DFT stand for on a coating specification?
Hot-dip galvanising coats steel with which metal?
What is the name of the hard, blue-grey oxide layer left on hot-rolled steel by the steel mill?
A paint covers 8 m² per litre in theory. How many litres are needed, in theory, to coat 40 m²?
In what unit is paint film thickness normally measured?
What is the word for covering an area with tape, plugs or a guard so that no coating reaches it?
On a safety data sheet, what is the name of the lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to catch fire?
What name is given to the extra coat brushed onto welds, edges and corners to build up film thickness there?
What is the name for the light rust that forms quickly on freshly blasted or freshly washed steel?
A primer has 40% volume solids and no thinner is added. What wet film thickness, in µm, gives a dry film of 60 µm?
What name is given to the holes made in hollow sections so that air can escape and zinc can flow in and out during galvanising?
What is the usual name for the curing part that is mixed into the base of a two-pack epoxy paint?

essays.stem: Your team must prepare a welded steel staircase for a three-coat paint system. Describe how you would plan the preparation, from reading the specification to the moment the steel is ready to prime.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the coating specification and the paint maker's data sheets and safety data sheets, so I know the surface standard, the film thicknesses, the drying times and the hazards. I inspect the staircase and list the weld and edge faults to dress. I plan the order of work: dressing welds and edges, degreasing, then blast or power-tool cleaning as the specification says, then dust removal, masking and priming. I book the blast booth and its trained operator if blasting is needed. I plan the space, lifting and access, the ventilation and the drying area, and keep hot work away from the paint area. I check the weather and shop readings each day and the equipment. I give each team member a task, brief them on the safety points and set hold points where I inspect and sign before the next step. Finally I make sure enough paint, thinner and PPE is in stock.
markingPoints: Reads the specification, data sheets and SDS first
Inspects the job and plans the order: dress, degrease, clean, mask, prime
Arranges blasting only in the booth by trained people, if needed
Plans space, ventilation, separation from hot work and drying area
Sets roles, hold points and checks, and confirms materials and PPE are ready

essays.stem: Describe the faults on a welded fabrication that should be put right before it is coated, and explain why each one matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Weld spatter must be removed, because paint pulls thin over the small balls and they can break off later, leaving bare steel. Slag must be chipped and brushed off every weld, because no coating sticks to it. Undercut, pinholes and porosity at the surface should be repaired or ground smooth, because paint bridges over them and leaves holes where rust starts. Sharp edges and flame-cut edges should be ground to a small radius, because paint draws away from a sharp edge and the film there is thin. Rough flame-cut edges also hold hard scale. Laminations or slivers on the plate surface should be ground out. Gaps and crevices, such as between back-to-back angles with skip welds, should be sealed or welded, because water and salt get in and paint cannot reach. Weld fumes and anti-spatter residues should be washed off as they stop the paint gripping.
markingPoints: Spatter and slag removed, with reasons
Undercut, porosity or pinholes repaired or ground
Sharp and flame-cut edges rounded, with reason
Crevices and gaps sealed or welded
Residues, laminations or slivers dealt with

essays.stem: Explain what relative humidity, dew point and steel temperature mean for coating work, how they are measured, and how you decide whether coating may start.
essays.modelAnswer: Relative humidity is how much moisture the air holds compared with the most it can hold at that temperature. The dew point is the temperature at which that moisture condenses as water on a surface. If the steel is at or near the dew point, a thin film of water forms on it, which you may not see, and paint over it will not stick and rust can start. I measure the air temperature and humidity with a sling psychrometer or a digital hygrometer and work out the dew point from tables or the instrument. I measure the steel temperature with a contact thermometer on the steel itself. The usual rule is that the steel must be at least 3 °C above the dew point, and the humidity and temperatures must be inside the limits on the paint data sheet. If they are not, I wait, move the work or improve the conditions, and I record all the readings.
markingPoints: Explains relative humidity and dew point correctly
Explains why water on the steel spoils the coating
Names instruments for air, humidity and steel temperature
States the rule: steel 3 °C above the dew point and inside data sheet limits
Says what to do if out of limits and records the readings

essays.stem: Compare hand and power tool cleaning with abrasive blast cleaning as ways of preparing steel for coating. Say when each is suitable and what safety rules apply.
essays.modelAnswer: Hand and power tool cleaning uses wire brushes, scrapers, grinders, flap discs and power wire wheels. It removes loose rust, loose scale and old flaking paint, but it leaves tight mill scale and gives little surface profile, and it can polish the steel smooth. It suits small areas, touch-up repairs, site work and paints that the data sheet says will tolerate it. Abrasive blast cleaning throws grit or shot at the steel at high speed. It removes all mill scale and rust and leaves a rough profile that high-performance primers need, so it is used where the specification asks for a high standard. For power tools the user wears eye and face protection, gloves, hearing protection and a dust mask, keeps guards on and checks the disc speed. Blasting is done only in a proper blast booth by trained people wearing an air-fed helmet and protective suit, because the dust and rebound are dangerous.
markingPoints: Describes hand and power tool cleaning and its limits
Describes blast cleaning and the profile it gives
Says when each is suitable, linked to the specification
Gives the PPE and guard rules for power tools
States blasting only in a proper booth by trained people with suitable PPE

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare a two-pack epoxy primer for use, following the maker's data sheet, from opening the tins to the start of application.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the data sheet and safety data sheet and put on chemical gloves, eye protection and a suitable respirator, in a ventilated area away from sparks. I check that the base and hardener are the right products, from matching batches, and inside their shelf life. I stir the base well with a mixer until all settled solids are mixed back. I measure the hardener to the exact mixing ratio on the data sheet, by volume or weight, and never guess or use part tins unless I measure them. I add it to the base and mix thoroughly, scraping the sides. If the data sheet gives an induction time, I let it stand for that time. I add thinner only of the type and amount allowed. I note the time of mixing, because the pot life starts then, and mix only what can be used before it runs out. I record the batch numbers and mixing time on the coating record.
markingPoints: Reads data sheet and SDS; PPE and ventilation in place
Checks products, batches and shelf life
Stirs the base and adds hardener at the exact ratio
Allows induction time and thins only as allowed
Notes the mixing time and pot life, mixes only what can be used, records batches

essays.stem: Explain the hazards of preparing and applying solvent-based coatings in a fabrication shop, and how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Solvent vapour can catch fire or explode, so paint is mixed and applied away from welding, grinding and other sparks, with no smoking, and an extinguisher is at hand. Paint and thinner are stored in a cool, ventilated store and lids are kept on. Vapour is also harmful to breathe, causing headaches and dizziness, and some hardeners cause allergies, so the area is well ventilated, with extraction if needed, and workers wear the respirator the SDS asks for. Paint on the skin can cause rashes, so chemical gloves and overalls are worn and skin is washed before eating. Splashes can hurt the eyes, so eye protection is worn and an eyewash is ready; an eye splash is rinsed with clean water for several minutes and first aid is called. Airless spray can inject paint into the skin, so guards and trigger locks are used. Soaked rags go in a closed metal bin, and waste paint is disposed of as the SDS says.
markingPoints: Fire: keeps sparks away, stores safely, extinguisher ready
Vapour: ventilation and the right respirator from the SDS
Skin and eyes: gloves, overalls, eye protection, correct first aid
Spray equipment risks controlled as the maker says
Waste and rags disposed of safely as the SDS says

essays.stem: Explain how a welded frame should be designed and prepared before it is sent for hot-dip galvanising, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Every closed hollow section must have vent and drain holes, placed at the ends and corners as the galvaniser advises, so air and moisture can escape and zinc can flow in and out. Without them, trapped air or water turns to steam in the molten zinc and the section can burst, which is dangerous, and the inside is left uncoated. Lapped joints and overlapping plates should be fully sealed by welding or left with a wide enough gap, because acid from cleaning can be trapped and weep out later. All slag and spatter must be removed from the welds, because zinc does not coat slag. Silicone anti-spatter sprays, paint marks and oil must be kept off or removed, as the galvaniser's cleaning will not lift them. The frame should be sized to fit the bath, with lifting points, and threads or holes that must stay clear are marked so the galvaniser can treat them.
markingPoints: Vent and drain holes in all hollow sections
Explains the risk of bursting and uncoated insides
Seals or gaps lapped joints so acid is not trapped
Removes slag, spatter, paint marks, oil and silicone sprays
Checks bath size and lifting points, marks threads or areas to protect

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the amount of primer to order for a job. Work the example: 30 m² of steel, primer of 50% volume solids, 75 µm dry film thickness and 30% losses.
essays.modelAnswer: First I work out the area of steel to be coated from the drawings, using the surface area per metre of each section, and add the plates. Then I take the volume solids and the dry film thickness from the specification and data sheet. The theoretical coverage in square metres per litre is the volume solids percentage times 10, divided by the dry film thickness in microns. Here that is 50 × 10 ÷ 75, which is about 6.67 m² per litre. The theoretical amount is the area divided by the coverage: 30 ÷ 6.67 = 4.5 litres. In practice some paint is lost in spray, on brushes, in the pot and on rough surfaces, so I add the loss allowance: 4.5 × 1.3 = 5.85 litres. I would order 6 litres, in whole tins, and check that it can all be used inside its shelf life. The same is done for each coat in the system.
markingPoints: Works out the area from the drawings
Uses coverage = volume solids × 10 ÷ DFT
Correct coverage of about 6.67 m² per litre and 4.5 litres in theory
Adds 30% loss to about 5.85 litres and orders 6 litres in whole tins
Repeats for each coat and considers shelf life

essays.stem: Describe the inspections you would carry out and record before you allow priming to start on a prepared steel frame.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that every weld and edge fault has been dressed and that there is no slag, spatter or sharp edge left. I check that oil and grease are gone, for example with a water-break test or a clean rag. I compare the cleaned surface with the standard in the specification, using the reference photos, and measure the surface profile with replica tape or a gauge if the steel was blasted. If the steel was near the sea, I test for soluble salts if the specification asks. I check that dust has been removed, using clear tape pressed on the surface. I measure the air temperature, humidity, dew point and steel temperature, and check that masking is in place. I check the paint batch, shelf life and the equipment. I write every reading, the time and my name on the coating record, and sign the hold point so the team may start priming.
markingPoints: Checks weld and edge dressing and freedom from oil
Checks cleanliness against the standard and the surface profile
Checks salts and dust where required
Measures and records the weather and steel readings and masking
Records all results, signs the hold point before priming

essays.stem: You lead four trainees preparing a set of steel brackets for coating. Explain how you would brief and supervise them through the day.
essays.modelAnswer: At the start I brief the team at the job. I show them the coating specification and the parts of the data sheets and SDS that matter, and explain the standard the brackets must reach. I give each person a clear task, for example two dressing welds and edges, one degreasing and cleaning, and one taking the weather readings and setting up the masking and the mixing area. I go over the hazards: grinding sparks kept away from the paint area, PPE for grinding and for paint, ventilation, and what to do in a spill or splash. I agree the hold points where I will inspect before the next stage. During the day I check work at each hold point, coach anyone who is struggling, and stop work if the conditions go out of limits. At the end, I make sure the area is cleaned, waste is disposed of correctly, the records are complete and the team knows what is next.
markingPoints: Explains the specification and data sheet points to the team
Gives each member a clear task
Briefs hazards, PPE and emergency actions
Inspects at hold points, coaches and stops work if out of limits
Ensures clean-up, waste disposal and complete records

practical1.title: Prepare a welded steel frame for coating: dress welds and edges, clean, mask and record the conditions
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a welded steel frame (for example a small gate frame or stand) with typical faults: spatter, slag, sharp edges and some undercut, and a short coating specification. As a group, read the specification and the data sheet and SDS for the primer and cleaner, and write a short preparation plan with each member's task and the hold points. Each member dresses part of the frame: removes spatter and slag, rounds sharp and flame-cut edges and repairs or grinds out faults as the assessor allows. Then degrease the frame with the cleaner named in the plan, power-tool clean it to the standard given, and remove the dust. One member measures and records the air temperature, humidity, dew point and steel temperature. Mask the areas the specification names. Finally, each member brushes a stripe coat of primer on part of the welds and edges, only if the conditions are inside the limits. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the plan and the record sheet to the group's practical.
materials: A welded steel frame with typical faults, and a short coating specification from the assessor
The primer's data sheet and SDS, and the cleaner's SDS
Angle grinders with flap discs and wire cup brushes, chipping hammers, scrapers and files
Solvent or water-based degreaser and clean rags
Sling psychrometer or digital hygrometer, dew point table and contact thermometer
Masking tape and plugs, primer, brushes, and a closed metal waste bin
Preparation plan sheet and coating record sheet
photos: The group's written preparation plan with tasks and hold points
The frame's faults before work, marked with chalk
Members dressing welds and edges in full PPE
The dressed frame after degreasing and cleaning
The weather and steel temperature readings being taken
The stripe coat on welds and edges
The completed record sheet and the cleaned work area
checklist: Read the specification, data sheet and SDS and helped write the plan
Wore the right PPE for grinding and for cleaning and painting
Removed spatter and slag and rounded sharp edges to the standard given
Degreased before power-tool cleaning and removed the dust
Measured or checked the conditions and decided correctly whether priming could start
Brushed an even stripe coat onto welds and edges
Cleaned up, put rags in the metal bin and completed the record
safety: Keep grinding sparks well away from paint, cleaner and rags; no hot work near the coating area
Wear face shield, eye protection, hearing protection and gloves when grinding; check guards and disc speed
Read the SDS and use the gloves, eye protection and respirator it calls for; keep the area well ventilated
Keep lids on paint and solvent, and keep a suitable extinguisher at hand
Put soaked rags in a closed metal bin and wash hands before eating

practical2.title: Plan the materials for a coating job, then mix a two-pack primer and check the wet film on test panels
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a drawing of a small steel structure and the data sheet and SDS for a two-pack primer. As a group, work out the area to be coated, the theoretical coverage from the volume solids and dry film thickness, the litres needed with an allowance for losses, and the number of tins to order. Write this on an estimate sheet. Then set up a mixing and coating area: ventilation, a spill kit, an extinguisher, the PPE named in the SDS, and no hot work nearby. Check the shop conditions and record them. One member checks the batch numbers and shelf life; two members measure and mix a small amount of primer at the exact ratio, allow the induction time and note the mixing time. Each member then applies primer by brush or roller to a prepared test panel, measures the wet film with a comb straight away and adjusts to reach the target wet film thickness. Finally, clean the tools as the data sheet says and dispose of waste correctly. Photograph each stage and add the photos, the estimate sheet and the record to the group's practical.
materials: Drawing of a small steel structure, with section sizes
Two-pack primer (or a single-pack primer if the Centre has none), with its data sheet and SDS
Measuring jugs or scales, mixing sticks or a power mixer, and a timer
Prepared steel test panels, about 300 mm × 300 mm, one per member
Brushes or rollers, wet film thickness combs, and the thinner the data sheet names
Hygrometer and contact thermometer, spill kit, extinguisher, closed metal waste bin
Estimate sheet and coating record sheet
photos: The completed estimate sheet with the area, coverage and litres
The mixing and coating area set up, with ventilation and extinguisher
The tins showing batch numbers and shelf life being checked
The base and hardener being measured to the ratio
A wet film comb reading on a panel
The cleaned tools, waste bin and completed coating record
checklist: Worked out the area, coverage and quantity correctly with losses
Helped set up a safe, ventilated coating area with no hot work nearby
Wore the PPE the SDS names
Checked batch numbers, shelf life and conditions and recorded them
Measured and mixed to the exact ratio and noted the mixing time and pot life
Applied an even coat and measured the wet film straight away
Adjusted application to reach the target wet film thickness
Cleaned tools and disposed of waste as the data sheet and SDS say
safety: Follow the maker's data sheet and SDS for every product
Mix and apply only in a well-ventilated area, with no welding, grinding or smoking nearby
Wear chemical gloves, eye protection and the respirator the SDS names
Know where the eyewash is; rinse any splash in the eye with clean water and report it
Keep lids on, keep an extinguisher and spill kit ready, and put waste in a closed metal bin
